intro_en:
"Arava, endless Arava... no juniper, no thistle, no tree...", as the song goes. The Israel National Trail continues on its way south through the landscapes of the Arava.

 Sapir - Tzukim (46)
 Nahal Barak - Nahal Tzihor (48)
character_en: Easy, mostly flat walking on dirt roads. Most of the walk is through terrain exposed to the sun.
transport_en: At the starting point: the community of Tzukim or the Arava road at the turn-off to Tzukim. At the end point: the Nahal Barak campsite is not accessible by public transport.
pois_en: Nahal Ashush. Ma'ale Ashush. The "turtle" bulbous rocks.
important_en: The entrance to the Nahal Barak overnight campsite is suitable for any vehicle. There is no water at the overnight campsite.
The segment does not include the Barak Canyon.
In Tzukim there are options for stocking up on water and food.
description_en:
The starting point of the segment is near the community of Tzukim - the youngest of the central Arava communities, founded in 2004 on the initiative of a group of people from the centre of the country who wanted to establish a community in the Arava focused mainly on tourism. In Tzukim you can stock up on water and food.
Setting out from Tzukim, we walk about 700 m north alongside the Arava road, then return to the Israel National Trail route along a green-marked jeep track that climbs up Nahal Ashush.
After about an hour of walking, the channel of Nahal Ashush narrows and the distance between the rock walls on either side shrinks. On emerging into a wider area, Nahal Ashush turns 90 degrees to the south, and this is where we meet the Israel National Trail route. To the right of the meeting point, two acacia trees grow beside the channel wall - a pleasant place for a rest stop.
The name Ashush, like other unique names in the area, raises the question: who decides the Hebrew names of streams, mountains and other geographical features? The story begins in the early days of the state, on the initiative of the first prime minister, David Ben-Gurion, who promoted the use of Hebrew names, including on maps of the country. In 1949 the Committee for Assigning Hebrew Names in the Negev was established, with 13 members - experts in geography, history and archaeology. During its ten months of activity, 533 geographical names were assigned within the Negev, and they appeared shortly afterwards on a map of the area produced by the Survey Department.
The formula for assigning names was as follows: first, the use of biblical and historical names; next, translation of the Arabic name; and as a last resort, giving a Hebrew form to Arabic names based on the similarity of words and sounds. Where necessary, new symbolic names were given. In this case, the stream's Arabic name is Wadi Ishishiya, and here a word with a Hebrew sound was sought, made up of the same letters as the Arabic name. As far as is known, the word Ashush has no meaning.
On reaching the Israel National Trail route, we turn left and head south-west on a red-marked jeep track, following the continuation of the Nahal Ashush channel. In this section the channel is up to several hundred metres wide.
Note: the trail markings in this section may have been damaged by flash floods in the stream. After about 2.5 km of walking, the main channel of Nahal Ashush turns once more at a 90-degree angle, towards the south-west. Because of the width of the channel, it is possible to miss the turn.
At the turning point, a black-marked road heads up the stream to the Mishor plateau, which spreads out on both sides of Road 40. The Israel National Trail continues south-west with the red markings.
We continue walking for about another 1.5 km along the jeep track in the wide channel, which forms a fan of Nahal Ashush tributaries - and reach Ma'ale Ashush.
The trail and the track turn south to the ascent. Tyre grooves in the ground, and perhaps also broken vehicle parts around the rock steps of the steep ascent, testify to the challenge it poses to the vehicles that climb it.
From the top of the ascent the trail heads south, advancing a long way through exposed terrain. The vegetation consists mainly of shrubs and dwarf shrubs growing in the channels. A shady spot that could hold a group is almost nonexistent.
After about 3.5 km of walking we reach a road junction. A green-marked road heads west to Nahal Tzofar, and the Israel National Trail continues south with the red markings.
After about another 1.5 km, a few solitary acacia trees appear near the trail, allowing a rest stop in broad shade.
We continue for about another hour of steady walking to the next trail junction, where a blue-marked road turns west to Nahal Za'af and Ramat Barak. A short distance further on there is another junction, where the Israel National Trail turns east towards the overnight campsite at Nahal Barak, along a green-marked trail. The overnight campsite is 1.5 km west of Road 90.
Here you can choose between two routes:
The short way is to continue with the green markings to the overnight campsite, a distance of about 2.5 km.
A slightly longer way leads to a special site - with turtle-shaped bulbous rocks. To reach it, continue south on the red-marked trail. After about half a kilometre of walking, to the right of the track, there is a concentration of bulbous rocks: an expanse full of rock domes shaped like giant turtles.
From the bulbous rocks you can return north to the point where the red trail meets the Israel National Trail. Alternatively, to avoid retracing your steps, you can continue south on the red trail to a T-junction - the meeting point with the Israel National Trail of segment 47 and with a blue-marked road that enters Nahal Barak. At the junction we turn left with the blue markings and head north-east to the overnight campsite. The extra walking is about 1.5 km.
author_en: Itzik Ben Dov, Trail Marking Coordinator, Society for the Protection of Nature in Israel (SPNI).
